fetched_contents.text: About Infectious Mononucleosis (Mono) | EBV and Mono * Infectious mononucleosis, also called “mono,” is a contagious disease. * Most people with mono get better in 2 to 4 weeks, but some may feel fatigued for several more weeks. * There is no vaccine to protect against infectious mononucleosis. What is it Infectious mononucleosis is a contagious disease most commonly caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). Other viruses can also cause this disease. Infectious mononucleosis is common among teenagers and young adults, especially college students. At least 1 out of 4 teenagers and young adults who get infected with EBV will develop infectious mononucleosis. Sign and symptoms When you feel sick Typical symptoms of infectious mononucleosis usually appear 4 to 6 weeks after you get infected with EBV. Symptoms may develop slowly and may not all occur at the same time. Symptoms of infectious mononucleosis include: * Extreme fatigue * Fever * Sore throat * Headaches and body aches * Swollen lymph nodes in the neck and armpits * Swollen liver or spleen or both * Rash Enlarged spleen and a swollen liver are less common symptoms. For some people, their liver or spleen or both may remain enlarged even after their fatigue ends. While most people get better in 2 to 4 weeks, some may feel fatigued for several more weeks. Occasionally, the symptoms of infectious mononucleosis can last for 6 months or longer. Causes and spread EBV is the most common cause of infectious mononucleosis, but other viruses can cause this disease. Typically, these viruses spread most commonly through bodily fluids, especially saliva. However, these viruses can also spread through blood and semen during sexual contact, blood transfusions, and organ transplantations. Other causes Other infections that can cause infectious mononucleosis include: * Cytomegalovirus (CMV) * Toxoplasmosis * HIV * Rubella * Hepatitis A, B, or C * Adenovirus Prevention There is no vaccine to protect against infectious mononucleosis. You can help protect yourself by not kissing people who have infectious mononucleosis; or sharing drinks, food, or personal items (like toothbrushes) with them. Testing and diagnosis Healthcare providers typically diagnose infectious mononucleosis based on symptoms. Laboratory tests are not usually needed to diagnose infectious mononucleosis. However, specific tests may be needed for patients who do not have a typical case of infectious mononucleosis. The blood work of patients who have infectious mononucleosis due to EBV infection may show: * More white blood cells (lymphocytes) than normal * Unusual looking white blood cells (atypical lymphocytes) * Fewer than normal neutrophils or platelets * Abnormal liver function Treatment and recovery Most people get better in 2 to 4 weeks. You can help relieve symptoms of infectious mononucleosis by: * Drinking fluids to stay hydrated * Getting plenty of rest * Taking over-the-counter medications for pain and fever Do not take penicillin antibiotics If you have infectious mononucleosis, you should not take penicillin antibiotics like ampicillin or amoxicillin. Based on the severity of the symptoms, a healthcare provider may recommend treatment of specific organ systems affected by infectious mononucleosis. Avoid contact sports Because your spleen may become enlarged as a result of infectious mononucleosis, you should avoid contact sports until you fully recover. Participating in contact sports can be strenuous and may cause the spleen to rupture. May 9, 2024

This activity reviews the cause, pathophysiology, and presentation of mononucleosis and highlights the role of the interprofessional team in its management. Objectives: * Describe the pathophysiology of mononucleosis. * Review the presentation of mononucleosis. * Summarize the treatment of mononucleosis. * Outline the importance of improving care coordination among interprofessional team members to improve outcomes for patients affected by mononucleosis. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic. Introduction Mononucleosis classically presents with fever, lymphadenopathy, and tonsillar pharyngitis. The term “infectious mononucleosis” was first used in the 1920s to describe a group of students with a similar pharyngeal illness and blood laboratory findings of lymphocytosis and atypical mononuclear cells. It was only later that Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was established as the cause of mononucleosis after an exposed healthcare worker developed a positive heterophile test.[1][2] Etiology The cause of mononucleosis is the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). EBV is a type of herpesvirus spread by contact, typically with salivary secretions. The duration of oral shedding is not entirely clear, but high levels of shedding can continue for a median of 6 months after illness onset. Transmission is generally person-to-person, but EBV is not considered a highly contagious disease. [3] Besides EBV other causes include: * CMV * Adenovirus * Hepatitis A * HIV * Toxoplasma * Rubella Epidemiology It is estimated that up to 95% of adults in the world are eventually seropositive to EBV. Therefore, EBV is widely disseminated in all population groups. The traditional age group where peak incidence is noted, however, is in 15 to 24-year olds. Classically, the symptomatic infection is in adolescents, which is why laypersons may refer to the infection as the “kissing disease.” Mononucleosis is uncommon in adults: approximately 2% of all pharyngeal disease in adults is attributable to this disease. Adults are generally not susceptible to clinical illness because of previous exposure. In the United States, clinically evident infection occurs at rates estimated at 30 times higher in whites than in blacks. One explanation for this disparity is that if acquired at a young (childhood) age, EBV is often subclinical. This would suggest earlier EBV exposures in blacks, and a higher frequency of asymptomatic infection as young children. [1][4] After exposure, the EBV infects the epithelial cells of the salivary glands and the oropharynx. Lymphocytes residing in the tonsils get exposed to the virus and then enter the bloodstream. Lymphoid hyperplasia is common and may be seen as generalized lymphadenopathy, tonsillitis, and hepatosplenomegaly. The infection of the B-lymphocytes results in the production of immunoglobulins (heterophile antibodies). Pathophysiology When EBV is introduced into the oropharynx, the virus begins the replication process. There is a predilection for infection of the B-cells of lymphoid tissue. Subsequently, the infection spreads through the lymphatic system. The body reacts by developing antibodies against the virus. In 90% or more of cases, heterophile antibodies are produced in response to the infection with EBV. EBV is a lifelong infection with periodic reactivation. In poor immune response systems, there is a small risk of EBV-induced malignancy, such as Hodgkin lymphoma.[5][6] History and Physical Fever, sore throat, fatigue, and tender lymph nodes are classic findings on history-taking in infected individuals with mononucleosis. The incubation period for mononucleosis is long averaging 3-6 weeks and most patients do not recall the exposure. The classical triad is fever, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy. Additional complaints include a headache, general malaise, and poor oral intake. Unfortunately for some, fatigue can be persistent for months in select individuals. Lymphadenopathy is more common in the posterior cervical region. The pharyngitis is often heralded with tonsillar exudates. Petechial lesions on the palate occur infrequently. Also, splenomegaly is a key finding on physical in up to half of patients with active clinical mononucleosis. Identification is important in patients prone to future injury, e.g., active sports participants. Skin examination in some patients may infrequently reveal a nonspecific, generalized maculopapular rash. This is separate from the antibiotic-induced rash discussed below. Evaluation As always, initial evaluation should include airway assessment to determine that the airway is patent and there is no impending occlusion or compromise. In rare instances, abscess or edema can impede proper maintenance of the airway. Also, determination of hemodynamic stability is important to rule out concomitant splenic injury or rupture in the acute illness of mononucleosis. Laboratory evaluation most commonly will reveal lymphocytosis, with a lymphocyte differential often greater than 50%. Atypical lymphocytosis of greater than 10% can be seen on blood smear. A general leukocytosis and occasionally thrombocytopenia may also be appreciated. Imaging is generally not needed in the evaluation of mononucleosis. Mini-report on what to do next after negative strep and ongoing symptoms

After a negative rapid strep test, the next step depends on whether the symptoms are consistent with a viral cause or another bacterial/infectious cause. The evidence supports that a negative strep test may mean the symptoms are due to another infection, such as a virus, or a non-infectious cause [N4-R1][N4-R5]. It also says that if a strep test is negative, a follow-up throat culture can confirm infection, and providers may order more tests after ruling out strep throat [N4-R2][N6-R2]. However, the CDC notes that it is usually not necessary to do a throat culture after a negative rapid strep test because antibiotics are not needed and the likelihood of strep is low at that point [N6-R1].

Additional testing is indicated when symptoms are persistent, severe, or atypical. In the case of a sore throat, fatigue, swollen glands, and recent dorm exposure, the evidence suggests that the provider should consider viral pharyngitis, post-strep sequelae, or other causes rather than assuming strep alone [N4-R3][N6-R4]. The CDC also notes that viral infections are a more common cause of sore throat than strep bacteria, so a negative strep test does not rule out a viral cause [N6-R4]. If symptoms persist beyond 1 week or worsen, follow-up is appropriate, including reassessment and possibly expanded testing if new symptoms appear [N4-R2].

When to consider mononucleosis is tied to the clinical context and symptoms. The evidence strongly supports that mononucleosis should be suspected in adolescents or young adults with sore throat and significant fatigue, especially when there is recent exposure to others who may have infectious mononucleosis [N2-R4][N2-F2]. Mononucleosis is also associated with fever, swollen lymph nodes, fatigue, headaches, and in some cases swollen liver or spleen [N1-F1][N2-R2]. The CDC and StatPearls both emphasize that fever, sore throat, fatigue, and tender lymph nodes are classic findings in mononucleosis [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The key supporting criteria are recent exposure, persistent fatigue, swollen glands, and the absence of clear strep-specific findings despite a negative rapid test [N1-R4][N2-F2].

Differentiating from viral pharyngitis and other post-strep/other causes is important. Viral pharyngitis is more likely than strep in the absence of definitive strep findings, and the evidence notes that viral infections are a more common cause of sore throat than strep bacteria [N6-R4]. Post-strep symptoms such as fatigue and swollen glands can occur after strep, but they are not diagnostic on their own [N4-R3][N5-R1]. The CDC also notes that, after ruling out strep, the provider will probably order more tests to determine the cause [N6-R2]. So the provider should distinguish between a recent viral infection, a persistent post-strep course, and other bacterial or viral causes based on symptoms, exposure, and test results.

If symptoms persist beyond 1 week, follow-up should include reassessment and possibly further testing. The evidence supports repeating throat cultures or other tests if symptoms continue after a negative strep test [N4-R2][N6-R2]. The CDC also suggests that, after a negative rapid strep test, follow-up is appropriate only when symptoms remain or worsen [N6-R1]. In this case, the dorm exposure and recent positive cases among dormmates make persistent symptoms more concerning and warrant closer follow-up than would be expected for an uncomplicated viral sore throat [N1-R4][N2-F2].

Overall, the next steps are: (1) reassure that a negative strep test does not always mean no infection and that a follow-up throat culture may be reasonable [N4-R2][N6-R1], (2) consider viral pharyngitis and other causes rather than assuming strep [N4-R3][N6-R4], (3) consider mononucleosis if symptoms are persistent, fatigue is significant, and there is recent exposure [N2-R4][N2-F2], and (4) recommend follow-up if symptoms last more than a week or worsen [N4-R2][N6-R1].

Mini-report on the likelihood of mononucleosis versus other diagnoses

The evidence suggests that mononucleosis is more likely than other diagnoses when symptoms include fever, sore throat, fatigue, swollen lymph nodes, and a recent context of dorm exposure or close contact with others who may have infectious mononucleosis [N1-F1][N2-R4][N2-F2]. StatPearls explicitly states that mononucleosis classically presents with fever, lymphadenopathy, and tonsillar pharyngitis, and that the clinical triad is fever, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy [N2-F2]. It also notes that the incubation period is long and many patients do not recall the exposure, which is important because this can make diagnosis more challenging [N2-F2]. The CDC similarly lists fatigue, fever, sore throat, headaches, and swollen lymph nodes as key symptoms of mononucleosis [N1-F1][N2-R2]. The evidence therefore supports that these symptoms are highly suggestive of mononucleosis, especially in an adolescent or young adult [N2-R4][N2-F2].

If mononucleosis is suspected, the appropriate tests are not the same as for strep. The CDC notes that laboratory tests are not usually needed for a typical case of mononucleosis, but specific tests may be needed for atypical or unclear cases [N1-F1]. StatPearls emphasizes that the monospot (or heterophile antibody) test is the diagnostic test of choice and is nearly 100% specific for EBV-related mononucleosis, although its sensitivity is closer to 85% and may be falsely negative early in illness [N2-F2]. The CDC also says that blood work may show lymphocytosis, atypical lymphocytes, fewer neutrophils or platelets, and abnormal liver function [N1-F1]. These are important findings to support the diagnosis when symptoms are consistent.

The evidence also supports caution against overdiagnosis. The CDC and StatPearls both indicate that diagnostic testing is not usually needed in a typical case, and that a negative heterophile test early in illness may not rule out mononucleosis [N1-R1][N2-F2]. This means that overtesting can occur if the provider assumes EBV without sufficient clinical or laboratory support. In this patient’s case, because strep was already ruled out, mononucleosis should be considered, but only after the provider has evaluated whether the symptoms are more consistent with viral pharyngitis, post-strep sequelae, or another cause [N4-R3][N6-R4]. The evidence also suggests waiting for more information when the clinical picture is ambiguous or when symptoms are not clearly fitting the classic mononucleosis pattern [N1-R1][N2-F2].

Clinical context makes mononucleosis more likely when the patient is an adolescent or young adult, has recent dorm exposure, and has persistent fatigue, swollen glands, and fever with a sore throat [N1-F1][N2-R4][N2-F2]. It is less likely if the symptoms are acute, localized, and respond quickly to routine care, or if the patient has a history of prior EBV exposure or a chronic condition that explains the symptoms. The CDC notes that EBV is widespread, and many adults are already seropositive, so mononucleosis is uncommon in adults who are already exposed [N2-F2]. In contrast, the evidence supports that viral pharyngitis is more common than strep in sore throat, especially after a negative strep test [N6-R4]. Thus, the clinical context here—recent dorm exposure, multiple positive dormmates, persistent symptoms, and negative strep—makes mononucleosis a reasonable concern, but not the only possible diagnosis.

In summary, mononucleosis is most strongly suggested by fever, sore throat, fatigue, swollen lymph nodes, and recent exposure, especially in adolescents [N1-F1][N2-R4][N2-F2]. The appropriate tests are a monospot and, if needed, other blood work, but overdiagnosis should be avoided when the clinical picture is unclear or when the patient has a better-fitting alternative diagnosis [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The context of dorm exposure and multiple similar cases supports suspicion, but the provider should also keep viral pharyngitis and post-strep sequelae in the differential [N4-R3][N6-R4].

Mini-report on dorm outbreak management and close-contact guidance

For dorm outbreak management, the evidence supports a structured response that includes identification, isolation, and prevention measures. The CDC guideline on isolation precautions notes that exposure precautions and symptom-based monitoring are important in health care settings, and that susceptible patients may need precautions when exposed [N3-F3]. While the exact wording is health-care centered, the broader principle applies: dorm settings should isolate symptomatic individuals and monitor close contacts. The evidence also supports contact tracing as the process of identifying, assessing, and managing people exposed to a disease to prevent additional transmission [N7-R3]. This means the dorm should identify all students who had close contact with the infected person(s) and assess them for symptoms.

Close contacts should be advised if they had recent exposure to someone with infectious mononucleosis or strep, especially if they were in shared spaces, shared drinks, food, or personal items, or had direct contact with saliva [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F3]. The CDC also notes that EBV spreads through saliva and close contact, so dormmates, roommates, and people who shared personal items are at higher risk [N2-F2]. The evidence also supports that close contact precautions may include gloves and gowns if contact with the patient’s environment is likely [N3-R5]. For dorm management, this means advising exposed students to monitor for symptoms and avoid close contact with others until they are cleared.

Quarantine, isolation, or symptom-based precautions are appropriate depending on the disease and exposure. The evidence supports that quarantine for close contacts is a common public health response after a positive case [N7-R2][N7-R4]. The WHO/CDC guideline on quarantine also recommends 14 days of quarantine for close contacts after exposure [N7-R1]. For infectious mononucleosis, the CDC and StatPearls both note that it is not considered highly contagious, but it can spread through saliva and close contact [N2-F2][N3-R1]. So in a dorm setting, close contacts should be advised to quarantine or isolate if symptoms develop, and symptomatic students should isolate until they are no longer contagious [N7-R2][N3-F3]. Symptom-based precautions may be appropriate when the provider is still assessing whether the illness is viral, strep, or mononucleosis, because the clinical picture can be overlapping [N3-R1][N7-R3].

Prevention and reporting steps the dorm should take include isolating symptomatic students, identifying close contacts, and reporting to campus health services or local public health authorities [N3-R1][N7-R3][N7-R4]. The evidence also supports that outbreak response planning should include vigilance, communication, and preparedness [N3-R4]. In a dorm, this means establishing a reporting protocol so that new cases are identified quickly, and that contact tracing can begin promptly [N7-R3]. The dorm should also ensure that students avoid sharing personal items and that symptomatic individuals stay away from communal spaces until they are cleared [N2-F2][N3-R5]. For strep, isolation is especially important because the CDC notes that respiratory secretions are not infectious within 20 to 24 hours of illness, but droplet precautions may still be needed during the first few days [N3-R2]. For mononucleosis, the evidence supports that the illness can last weeks, and that students should avoid contact sports until fully recovered [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Interpreting dorm exposure in relation to mononucleosis and strep depends on the symptoms and test results. The patient’s recent dorm exposure and multiple positive dormmates make mononucleosis a plausible explanation, especially because EBV spreads through saliva and close contact [N2-F2][N3-R1]. However, the dorm also has strep cases, so strep should not be ignored. The evidence supports that a negative strep test does not rule out a viral cause, and that follow-up throat culture may be reasonable if symptoms persist [N4-R2][N6-R1]. Dorm exposure therefore raises both possibilities: mononucleosis may be more likely if symptoms are persistent, fatigue is significant, and the illness is not responding to routine care; strep may be more likely if symptoms are acute, localized, and improve with antibiotics [N4-R3][N6-R4]. The dorm should manage these exposures separately: isolate symptomatic students, trace close contacts, and report to campus health services so that each illness can be evaluated appropriately [N3-R1][N7-R3][N7-R4].

## Summary of the patient’s situation

A 19-year-old female from Redwood Hall presents with a 2-day history of acute sore throat and fever up to 101.2°F. She denies coughing, difficulty swallowing, or shortness of breath. A rapid strep test is negative, but three dormmates tested positive for strep. Two others have negative results but persistent sore throat and swollen glands. She describes cervical lymphadenopathy, fatigue, and mild headache. She is concerned about mononucleosis because of recent dorm exposure and wants guidance on diagnostic steps after a negative strep test and on managing multiple similar cases in the dorm.

## What should be done next after a negative strep test and ongoing symptoms?

### Additional testing is indicated when symptoms are persistent or atypical
A negative rapid strep test means the symptoms may not be caused by strep bacteria, but it does not rule out infection altogether [N4-R1][N4-R5]. The evidence says that if a strep test is negative, a follow-up throat culture may be used to confirm infection, and providers may order more tests after ruling out strep throat [N4-R2][N6-R2]. However, the CDC notes that it is usually not necessary to do a throat culture after a negative rapid strep test because antibiotics are not needed and the likelihood of strep is low at that point [N6-R1].

If symptoms persist, worsen, or are not improving as expected, follow-up is appropriate. The evidence supports that persistent symptoms, especially after a negative strep test, may warrant reassessment and possibly expanded testing [N4-R2][N6-R1]. In this case, the fact that the patient has ongoing sore throat, swollen glands, fatigue, and a recent dorm exposure makes follow-up especially reasonable [N1-R4][N2-F2].

### When to consider mononucleosis and what criteria support it
Mononucleosis should be considered when symptoms are persistent and when there is recent exposure to others who may have infectious mononucleosis. The evidence strongly supports that mononucleosis is more likely in adolescents or young adults with sore throat, fatigue, swollen glands, and recent exposure [N2-R4][N2-F2]. It also says that fever, sore throat, fatigue, and swollen lymph nodes are classic findings in mononucleosis [N1-F1][N2-R2]. The CDC notes that EBV is the most common cause of infectious mononucleosis, and that the illness can last weeks, with some people feeling fatigued for several more weeks [N1-F1][N2-F2].

The most supportive criteria for mononucleosis are:
- recent dorm exposure and shared living conditions,
- persistent fatigue,
- swollen glands,
- sore throat,
- fever,
- and, if available, swollen liver or spleen [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-F2].

### How to differentiate from viral pharyngitis and other causes
Viral pharyngitis is a more common cause of sore throat than strep bacteria, especially after a negative strep test [N6-R4]. The evidence also notes that post-strep symptoms such as fatigue and swollen glands can occur after strep, but they are not diagnostic on their own [N4-R3][N5-R1]. That means the provider should not assume mononucleosis simply because a sore throat and swollen glands persist after a negative strep test.

Instead, the provider should consider a broader differential:
- viral pharyngitis,
- post-strep sequelae,
- other viral infections,
- and, if appropriate, other bacterial causes [N4-R3][N5-R1][N6-R4].

The evidence also supports that the provider should reassess and consider other tests if symptoms remain or worsen [N4-R2][N6-R1].

### What follow-up should be done if symptoms persist beyond 1 week?
If symptoms persist beyond 1 week, the next step should include reassessment and possibly further testing. The evidence supports repeating throat cultures or other tests if symptoms continue after a negative strep test [N4-R2][N6-R2]. It also says that follow-up is appropriate when symptoms remain or worsen [N6-R1]. In this patient’s case, the dorm exposure and persistent symptoms make follow-up especially important [N1-R4][N2-F2].

## What is the likelihood of mononucleosis versus other diagnoses?

### Which symptoms most strongly suggest mononucleosis?
Mononucleosis is most strongly suggested by:
- fever,
- sore throat,
- fatigue,
- swollen lymph nodes,
- and recent exposure in a shared setting such as a dorm [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R4][N2-F2].

StatPearls emphasizes that mononucleosis classically presents with fever, lymphadenopathy, and tonsillar pharyngitis, and that the classical triad is fever, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy [N2-F2]. The CDC similarly lists fatigue, fever, sore throat, headaches, and swollen lymph nodes as key symptoms [N1-F1][N2-R2]. These symptoms are highly suggestive in an adolescent or young adult, especially after recent dorm exposure [N2-R4][N2-F2].

### What tests should be ordered if mononucleosis is suspected?
If mononucleosis is suspected, the evidence supports using the monospot (or heterophile antibody) test as the diagnostic test of choice. StatPearls notes that this test is nearly 100% specific for EBV-related mononucleosis, although its sensitivity is closer to 85% and it may be falsely negative early in illness [N2-F2]. The CDC also says that blood work may show lymphocytosis, atypical lymphocytes, fewer neutrophils or platelets, and abnormal liver function [N1-F1].

### How to avoid overdiagnosis and when to wait for more information
The evidence supports caution against overdiagnosis. The CDC and StatPearls both note that diagnostic testing is not usually needed in a typical case of mononucleosis, and that a negative heterophile test early in illness may not rule out mononucleosis [N1-R1][N2-F2]. That means the provider should not assume mononucleosis without sufficient clinical or laboratory support.

In this patient’s case, mononucleosis should be considered, but only after ruling out more common viral pharyngitis and post-strep sequelae [N4-R3][N6-R4]. If the clinical picture is unclear, the provider should wait for more information, including follow-up symptoms, exposure details, and test results before making a firm diagnosis [N1-R1][N2-F2].

### What clinical context makes mononucleosis more or less likely?
Mononucleosis is more likely when the patient is an adolescent or young adult, has recent dorm exposure, and has persistent fatigue, swollen glands, and fever with a sore throat [N1-F1][N2-R4][N2-F2]. The dorm should isolate symptomatic students and identify close contacts quickly. The evidence supports outbreak response planning that includes vigilance, communication, and preparedness [N3-R4]. In practice, this means:

- identifying and monitoring close contacts,

- avoiding sharing personal items,

Mini-report on what to do next after negative strep and ongoing symptoms

After a negative rapid strep test, the next step depends on whether the symptoms are consistent with a viral cause or another bacterial/infectious cause. The evidence supports that a negative strep test may mean the symptoms are due to another infection, such as a virus, or a non-infectious cause [N4-R1][N4-R5]. It also says that if a strep test is negative, a follow-up throat culture can confirm infection, and providers may order more tests after ruling out strep throat [N4-R2][N6-R2]. However, the CDC notes that it is usually not necessary to do a throat culture after a negative rapid strep test because antibiotics are not needed and the likelihood of strep is low at that point [N6-R1].

Additional testing is indicated when symptoms are persistent, severe, or atypical. In the case of a sore throat, fatigue, swollen glands, and recent dorm exposure, the evidence suggests that the provider should consider viral pharyngitis, post-strep sequelae, or other causes rather than assuming strep alone [N4-R3][N6-R4]. The CDC also notes that viral infections are a more common cause of sore throat than strep bacteria, so a negative strep test does not rule out a viral cause [N6-R4]. If symptoms persist beyond 1 week or worsen, follow-up is appropriate, including reassessment and possibly expanded testing if new symptoms appear [N4-R2].

When to consider mononucleosis is tied to the clinical context and symptoms. The evidence strongly supports that mononucleosis should be suspected in adolescents or young adults with sore throat and significant fatigue, especially when there is recent exposure to others who may have infectious mononucleosis [N2-R4][N2-F2]. Mononucleosis is also associated with fever, swollen lymph nodes, fatigue, headaches, and in some cases swollen liver or spleen [N1-F1][N2-R2]. The CDC and StatPearls both emphasize that fever, sore throat, fatigue, and tender lymph nodes are classic findings in mononucleosis [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The key supporting criteria are recent exposure, persistent fatigue, swollen glands, and the absence of clear strep-specific findings despite a negative rapid test [N1-R4][N2-F2].

Differentiating from viral pharyngitis and other post-strep/other causes is important. Viral pharyngitis is more likely than strep in the absence of definitive strep findings, and the evidence notes that viral infections are a more common cause of sore throat than strep bacteria [N6-R4]. Post-strep symptoms such as fatigue and swollen glands can occur after strep, but they are not diagnostic on their own [N4-R3][N5-R1]. The CDC also notes that, after ruling out strep, the provider will probably order more tests to determine the cause [N6-R2]. So the provider should distinguish between a recent viral infection, a persistent post-strep course, and other bacterial or viral causes based on symptoms, exposure, and test results.

If symptoms persist beyond 1 week, follow-up should include reassessment and possibly further testing. The evidence supports repeating throat cultures or other tests if symptoms continue after a negative strep test [N4-R2][N6-R2]. The CDC also suggests that, after a negative rapid strep test, follow-up is appropriate only when symptoms remain or worsen [N6-R1]. In this case, the dorm exposure and recent positive cases among dormmates make persistent symptoms more concerning and warrant closer follow-up than would be expected for an uncomplicated viral sore throat [N1-R4][N2-F2].

Overall, the next steps are: (1) reassure that a negative strep test does not always mean no infection and that a follow-up throat culture may be reasonable [N4-R2][N6-R1], (2) consider viral pharyngitis and other causes rather than assuming strep [N4-R3][N6-R4], (3) consider mononucleosis if symptoms are persistent, fatigue is significant, and there is recent exposure [N2-R4][N2-F2], and (4) recommend follow-up if symptoms last more than a week or worsen [N4-R2][N6-R1].

If symptoms persist, worsen, or are not improving as expected, follow-up is appropriate. The evidence supports that persistent symptoms, especially after a negative strep test, may warrant reassessment and possibly expanded testing [N4-R2][N6-R1]. In this case, the fact that the patient has ongoing sore throat, swollen glands, fatigue, and a recent dorm exposure makes follow-up especially reasonable [N1-R4][N2-F2].

Mononucleosis should be considered when symptoms are persistent and when there is recent exposure to others who may have infectious mononucleosis. It also says that fever, sore throat, fatigue, and swollen lymph nodes are classic findings in mononucleosis [N1-F1][N2-R2]. The CDC notes that EBV is the most common cause of infectious mononucleosis, and that the illness can last weeks, with some people feeling fatigued for several more weeks [N1-F1][N2-F2].

The most supportive criteria for mononucleosis are:
- recent dorm exposure and shared living conditions,
- persistent fatigue,
- swollen glands,
- sore throat,
- fever,
- and, if available, swollen liver or spleen [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-F2].

Viral pharyngitis is a more common cause of sore throat than strep bacteria, especially after a negative strep test [N6-R4]. Instead, the provider should consider a broader differential:
- viral pharyngitis,
- post-strep sequelae,
- other viral infections,
- and, if appropriate, other bacterial causes [N4-R3][N5-R1][N6-R4].

The evidence also supports that the provider should reassess and consider other tests if symptoms remain or worsen [N4-R2][N6-R1].

### What follow-up should be done if symptoms persist beyond 1 week?

The evidence supports repeating throat cultures or other tests if symptoms continue after a negative strep test [N4-R2][N6-R2]. It also says that follow-up is appropriate when symptoms remain or worsen [N6-R1]. In this patient’s case, the dorm exposure and persistent symptoms make follow-up especially important [N1-R4][N2-F2].
